unit_description: This unit teaches students to compare fractions that have the same numerator. Students use visual models, number lines, and reasoning, and explain why fractions must refer to the same whole.
unit_goals: Compare fractions with the same numerator using visual models.
Compare fractions with the same numerator on number lines.
Understand why fractions must refer to the same whole.
Compare fractions and explain the reasoning.
Understand that with like numerators, the smaller denominator names the larger fraction.

weeks.weekly_focus: Students compare fractions with the same numerator using models and number lines and explain that the whole must be the same size.

lessons.lesson_title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator Using Models
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by shading one or two parts of models with different denominators and comparing.
lessons.concept: When two fractions have the same numerator, they represent the same number of parts. The fraction with the smaller denominator has larger parts, so it is larger overall.
lessons.practice: Compare fractions with like numerators using area models.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions with the same numerator using models.

questions.hint: Halves are bigger pieces than fourths.
Fifths are smaller pieces than thirds.

learn.title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator Using Models
teaching_points: Same numerator means the same number of parts.
A smaller denominator means bigger parts.
Bigger parts make a larger amount.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.hint: Fourth pieces are bigger than eighth pieces.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Use visual models to compare each pair of fractions.

flashcards.title: Like Numerators Models
flashcards.instructions: Review comparing fractions with like numerators using models.

bigIdea.title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator Using Models
bigIdea.subtitle: Same number of bigger parts is more
bigIdea.intro: When the numerators are the same, you are counting the same number of parts. The fraction with the bigger parts has more total amount.

ruleCards.description: Both fractions count the same number of parts.
The smaller denominator means each part is bigger.

lessons.lesson_title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator on Number Lines
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by locating 1/2 and 1/4 on the same number line and comparing their positions.
lessons.concept: On a number line, the fraction with the same numerator but smaller denominator is farther from 1? Wait, farther from 0? Actually it's farther from 1? Let's think: 1/2 is at 0.5, 1/4 at 0.25. 1/2 is closer to 1 and farther from 0. The larger fraction is farther to the right. With same numerator, smaller denominator means larger value, so farther right. The number line makes this visible.
lessons.practice: Compare fractions with like numerators on number lines.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions with the same numerator on number lines.

questions.prompt: Which is farther to the right: 1/2 or 1/4?

questions.hint: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, 3/8 is less.

learn.title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator on Number Lines
teaching_points: Locate both fractions on the same number line.
The fraction farther right is larger.
With the same numerator, the smaller denominator is farther right.

example.prompt: Compare 3/4 and 3/8 on a number line.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Compare 2/3 and 2/6 on a number line.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Use number lines to compare each pair of fractions.

flashcards.title: Like Numerators Number Lines
flashcards.instructions: Review comparing fractions with like numerators on number lines.

bigIdea.title: Compare Fractions With the Same Numerator on Number Lines
bigIdea.subtitle: Farther right means larger
bigIdea.intro: A number line shows that fractions with the same numerator are not always the same amount. The fraction with smaller pieces is closer to 1? Wait, fractions with smaller pieces (larger denominator) are smaller. So the larger fraction is farther right. Good.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How does a number line show that 1/2 > 1/4?

ruleCards.description: 1/2 is farther to the right on the number line.

lessons.lesson_title: Understand Why Fractions Must Refer to the Same Whole
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by comparing shaded parts of rectangles that are the same size versus different sizes.
lessons.concept: You can only compare fractions when they refer to the same-sized whole. A half of a small pizza is not the same as a half of a large pizza.
lessons.practice: Identify when fractions refer to the same whole and when comparison is not fair.
lessons.objective: Understand that fractions must refer to the same whole to compare.

questions.prompt: Can you compare 1/2 of a small cookie and 1/2 of a large cookie?
To compare 1/3 and 2/3, must the wholes be the same size?
questions.hint: Yes, the same whole is needed.

questions.prompt: If two rectangles are different sizes, can you tell which 1/4 is larger?

learn.title: Understand Why Fractions Must Refer to the Same Whole
teaching_points: Fractions are parts of a whole.
If the wholes are different sizes, you cannot compare the fractions.
Always check that the whole is the same size.

example.prompt: Which is larger: 1/2 of a small square or 1/2 of a large square?
example.equation: Cannot compare because the wholes are different sizes.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Two pizzas are the same size. Maria ate 3/8 of one. Tom ate 3/8 of the other. Did they eat the same amount?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Tell whether each comparison is fair and explain.

bigIdea.title: Understand Why Fractions Must Refer to the Same Whole
bigIdea.subtitle: Same whole, fair comparison
bigIdea.intro: Comparing fractions only makes sense when the wholes are the same size. If the wholes are different, a fraction can mean a different amount.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: Why does 1/2 of a small cookie not equal 1/2 of a large cookie?

ruleCards.description: Fractions can be compared only when the wholes are the same.
A fraction of a larger whole is more than the same fraction of a smaller whole.

lessons.lesson_title: Compare Fractions and Explain the Reasoning
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by writing a sentence to explain a fraction comparison.
lessons.concept: To compare fractions, use models or number lines to see which is larger. Then explain the reason: same numerator means same number of parts, smaller denominator means bigger parts, so it's larger.
lessons.practice: Compare fractions and write or say a clear explanation.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions and explain the reasoning.

questions.hint: Same numerator; halves are larger than fourths.
Same numerator; fifths are smaller than thirds.

questions.correct_answer: 3/8 < 3/4 because eighths are smaller than fourths
questions.hint: Same numerator; smaller denominator means bigger pieces.

learn.title: Compare Fractions and Explain the Reasoning
teaching_points: Say that the numerators are the same.
Explain that the smaller denominator makes larger parts.

example.equation: 2/6 < 2/3 because thirds are larger pieces than sixths

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Compare 3/5 and 3/10 and explain your reasoning.
try_it.correct_answer: 3/5 > 3/10 because fifths are larger than tenths
try_it.hint: Same numerator; fifths are larger pieces.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Compare each pair and write a sentence explaining your reasoning.

bigIdea.title: Compare Fractions and Explain the Reasoning
bigIdea.subtitle: Use words to explain why
bigIdea.intro: A good explanation tells what is the same and what is different. With like numerators, the number of parts is the same. The difference is the size of each part.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How do you explain that 2/3 is larger than 2/5?

ruleCards.description: Both fractions count the same number of parts.
The fraction with larger parts is larger overall.

lessons.fact_drill: Rapid review of comparing like numerators with models, number lines, same whole, and reasoning.
lessons.concept: Review the four big ideas from this unit: comparing fractions with the same numerator using models, comparing on number lines, understanding the same whole, and explaining reasoning.
lessons.practice: Complete a balanced evaluation covering the skills from this unit.
lessons.objective: Show what you know about comparing fractions with like numerators.

warmup.instructions: Get ready to show what you know.

questions.prompt: Can you compare 1/4 of a small pizza and 1/4 of a large pizza?

learn.title: Ready to Show What You Know
teaching_points: Use any strategy that helps you.

bigIdea.title: Unit Evaluation: Fraction Comparison
bigIdea.subtitle: Show what you know
bigIdea.intro: This evaluation checks your understanding of the four big ideas from this unit: comparing fractions with like numerators using models, comparing on number lines, the same whole requirement, and explaining your reasoning.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: What do you know about comparing fractions with like numerators?

ruleCards.description: The fraction with the larger pieces is larger.
Fractions can only be compared if they refer to the same whole.
